title: REST API design principles
idea: A REST API exposes resources: a noun in the URL names the thing, the HTTP method names the action, and the status code reports the result.

analogy.text: A library catalogue. Every book has one fixed shelf address, your request slip says borrow or return, and the desk replies with a stamp.
analogy.breaks: A librarian remembers you; a REST server forgets you after each request.

points: A URL names a resource, a noun such as `/books/7`, never an action.
The method is the action: `GET` reads, `POST` creates, `DELETE` removes.
The status code is the result: `201` created, `404` not found.
Each request carries everything the server needs; it keeps no client state.

code.title: A /books API
code.caption: Express 5 serving `/books`, calling itself with `fetch`. Press Run for the real output.

walk.text: Keep books in memory; the next id starts at 2.
`GET` returns the list, or one book; a missing id gets 404.
`POST` stores the book and answers 201 with its new URL.
`DELETE` answers 204 with no body, or 404 if the id is unknown.
A helper sends one request and prints the method, path and status.
Create, read, delete, then read again. Close the server.

pitfalls: Keep verbs out of paths such as `/getBook` or `/deleteBook/7`; the method is the verb.
Do not mix `/book` and `/books`; choose plural and keep it everywhere.
Return `404` for a missing resource, not `200` with an error message.

quiz.why: The first delete removes the book, so 204. The second finds nothing, so 404.

takeaway: Nouns in the URL, verbs in the method, results in the status.
